Both TNF-induced apoptosis and necroptosis 
(obtained in the presence of the chemical pan-caspase 
inhibitor Z‑VAD.fmk) are blocked in TRADD-deficient 
cells58

Moreover, RNAi-mediated 
knockdown of TRADD stimulates (rather than inhibits) 
the formation of complex II in some cell types, suggest­
ing that TRADD is not required for the assembly and 
function of complex II (REFS 56,59).

experiment.perturbation: TRADD deficiency or RNAi knockdown; SMAC mimetics; Z-VAD.fmk

text: RIP3 expression correlates with cells' ability to respond to TNF plus Z-VAD.fmk by necroptosis, and cells stably or temporarily depleted of RIP3 show that this kinase is required for necroptosis and for a RIP1- and RIP3-containing complex assembled in response to TNF and stabilized by SMAC mimetics or caspase inhibitors.

quotes.quote:
others 
respond to TNF plus Z‑VAD.fmk by activating necrop­
tosis60, a phenomenon that has recently been correlated 
with the expression of RIP3 (REF. 11).

Recent experiments with cells that have been stably or 
temporarily depleted of RIP3 showed that this kinase is 
required for necroptosis and revealed the existence of a 
RIP1- and RIP3‑containing complex that is assembled 
in response to TNF and is stabilized in the presence of 
SMAC mimetics or caspase inhibitors10–12.

experiment.perturbation: stable or transient RIP3 depletion; TNF plus Z-VAD.fmk, SMAC mimetics
experiment.measurement: necroptotic death and RIP1–RIP3 complex assembly

quotes.quote:
Necroptosis induced by 
CD95L, TRAIL or TNF in combination with Z‑VAD.fmk 
is abrogated in RIP1‑deficient T cells9, and enforced 
dimerization of RIP1 can induce necroptosis in FADD-
deficient Jurkat lymphocytes7.

experiment.perturbation: death-ligand stimulation with Z-VAD.fmk; enforced RIP1 dimerization
experiment.measurement: necroptotic cell death

text: Mice lacking RIP1 display extensive apoptosis in lymphoid and adipose tissues and die 1–3 days after birth.

mice 
lacking RIP1 display extensive apoptosis in lymphoid 
and adipose tissues and die 1–3 days after birth62.

experiment.perturbation: genetic RIP1 deletion
experiment.measurement: tissue apoptosis and postnatal survival

text: Necroptosis involves mutual RIP1 and RIP3 kinase activity including autophosphorylation of RIP1 on Ser161 and RIP3-mediated phosphorylation of RIP1; however, murine cytomegalovirus infection induces RIP3-dependent but RIP1-independent necroptosis and overexpression of catalytically active RIP3 triggers necroptosis irrespective of RIP1.

involving the autophosphorylation of RIP1 on Ser161 
and direct or indirect RIP3‑mediated phosphorylation 
of RIP1 (REFS 11,63). Recently, murine cytomegalovirus 
infection was shown to induce RIP3‑dependent but 
RIP1‑independent necroptosis66. Moreover, overexpres­
sion of catalytically active RIP3 can trigger necroptosis 
irrespective of the presence of RIP1 (REF. 12).

experiment.perturbation: viral infection; overexpression of catalytically active RIP3; RIP1 absence
experiment.measurement: phosphorylation sites and necroptosis induction

text: PARP1 overactivation is critically involved in the necroptotic response of L929 fibrosarcoma cells to TNF and eventually results in depletion of ATP and NAD; RIP1-deficient and TRAF2-deficient MEFs are resistant to PARP1-induced cell death from DNA alkylating agents, indicating RIP1 can act downstream of PARP1.

quotes.quote:
The 
overactivation of PARP1, perhaps due to ROS-mediated 
DNA damage, is critically involved in the necroptotic 
response of L929 fibrosarcoma cells to TNF72 and even­
tually results in the depletion of ATP and NAD

Surprisingly, both RIP1‑deficient and TRAF2-deficient 
MEFs are resistant to PARP1‑induced cell death in 
response to DNA alkylating agents80, indicating that RIP1 
activation can also occur downstream of PARP1

experiment.perturbation: TNF treatment; DNA alkylating agents
experiment.measurement: necroptotic cell death, ATP and NAD levels

text: Harlequin mice, bearing a hypomorphic Aifm1 mutation with reduced AIF, are protected against several necrotic stimuli including brain ischaemia–reperfusion injury, and pharmacological and genetic PARP1 inhibition has cytoprotective effects.

quotes.quote:
Harlequin 
mice, which bear a hypomorphic mutation of Aifm1 and 
therefore express reduced amounts of AIF, are protected 
against several necrotic stimuli, including ischaemia–
reperfusion injury of the brain76–78. Similarly, pharmaco­
logical and genetic inhibition of PARP1 has consistent 
cytoprotective effects79.

experiment.perturbation: hypomorphic Aifm1 mutation; pharmacological/genetic PARP1 inhibition
experiment.measurement: protection against necrotic stimuli/ischaemia–reperfusion injury

text: Mitochondria show transiently increased mitochondrial transmembrane potential during the early phases of necroptosis, consistent with a RIP1-dependent inhibition of adenine nucleotide translocase.

This model is apparently corroborated by the 
fact that mitochondria show transiently increased Δψm 
during the early phases of necroptosis15,24.

experiment.perturbation: necroptosis induction (observational within dying cells)
experiment.measurement: mitochondrial transmembrane potential (Δψm)

text: Genetic ablation of Ppif (encoding CYPD), but not of genes coding for all known VDAC and ANT isoforms, consistently protects mice against ischaemic injury of the brain and heart in vivo.

quotes.quote:
CYPD seems to 
be the leading player of the PTPC, as genetic ablation 
of peptidylprolyl isomerase F (Ppif; the CYPD-encoding 
gene), but not of the genes coding for all known VDAC 
and ANT isoforms83,84, consistently protects mice against 
ischaemic injury of the brain and heart in vivo20,21.

experiment.system: mice with genetic ablation of Ppif, VDAC or ANT isoforms
experiment.perturbation: gene knockout
experiment.measurement: protection against ischaemic brain and heart injury in vivo

text: RIP3 physically interacts with and allosterically activates the metabolic enzymes PYGL, GLUL and GLUD1, and RNAi knockdown of any of these enzymes attenuates TNF plus Z-VAD.fmk-mediated ROS production and necroptosis.

quotes.quote:
RIP3 physically inter­
acts with and allosterically activates several metabolic 
enzymes, including glycogen phosphorylase (PYGL), 
glutamate–ammonia ligase (GLUL) and glutamate 
dehydrogenase 1 (GLUD1). RNAi-mediated knock­
down of any of these enzymes attenuates TNF plus 
Z-VAD.fmk-mediated ROS production and necrop­
tosis12.

experiment.perturbation: RNAi knockdown of PYGL, GLUL or GLUD1

text: ROS production by mitochondrial respiratory complex I is crucial for the necrotic response of L929 cells to TNF, though ROS production is not essential for all instances of TNF-induced necrosis.

the Fiers 
group showed that ROS production by mitochondrial 
respiratory complex I is crucial for the necrotic response 
of L929 cells to TNF85.

Although 
ROS production is not essential for all instances of TNF-
induced necrosis11,86

experiment.perturbation: TNF treatment with manipulation of mitochondrial respiratory complex I

text: siRNA-mediated downregulation of NOX1 almost abrogates TNF-induced ROS generation but only marginally rescues L929 fibrosarcoma cells from necroptosis, and ROS scavengers such as BHA exert anti-necroptotic effects in some but not all experimental settings.

quotes.quote:
NOX1‑derived ROS are not a 
requisite for necroptosis, as shown by the fact that small 
interfering RNA-mediated downregulation of NOX1 
almost abrogates TNF-induced ROS generation but only 
marginally rescues L929 fibrosarcoma cells from necrop­
tosis16. Accordingly, ROS scavengers such as tert-butyl-
4‑hydroxyanisole (BHA) exert anti-necroptotic effects 
in some (but not all) experimental settings95,96.

text: NOX1 activation downstream of TNFR1 depends on riboflavin kinase, which physically bridges the TNFR1 death domain and p22phox, and NOX1 is activated within minutes of TNF administration.

quotes.quote:
NOX1 activation is dependent on ribo­flavin 
kinase, which physically bridges the TNFR1 death 
domain and p22phox (also known as CYBA), the com­
mon subunit of multiple NADPH oxidases17. NOX1 is 
activated within minutes of the administration of TNF

text: TNF stimulates ROS formation via JNK1-dependent degradation of ferritin and elevation of the labile iron pool; ferritin-deficient cells are more resistant to TNF-induced labile iron pool elevation, ROS generation and necroptosis than wild-type cells, and RIP1-deficient MEFs fail to elevate the labile iron pool on TNF administration.

iron storage capacity is reduced) are more resistant to 
TNF-induced labile iron pool elevation, ROS genera­
tion and necroptosis than their wild-type counterparts99.

the labile iron pool on TNF administration99

text: Nitration of the mitochondrial complex I subunit NDUFB8 elicits RIP1- and RIP3-mediated necroptosis, while nitrite attenuates oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, hypothermia, tissue infarction and organismal death in a murine model of TNF-induced shock.

quotes.quote:
Recently, nitra­
tion has been shown to elicit RIP1- and RIP3‑mediated 
necroptosis, with respiratory complex I subunit NDUFB8 
being involved103. This is apparently in contrast with the 
well-known cytoprotective effects of nitrite, which attenu­
ates oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage and dysfunc­
tion, hypothermia, tissue infarction and organismal death 
in a murine model of TNF-induced shock104.

verdict_note: The paper states only that 'nitration has been shown to elicit RIP1- and RIP3-mediated necroptosis, with respiratory complex I subunit NDUFB8 being involved'; the claim sharpens this into nitration of NDUFB8 itself being the eliciting event, a specificity the excerpt does not assert. Treatment of 
L929 cells with TNF leads to PLA2 activation, and over­
expression of cPLA2 sensitizes TNF-resistant L929 vari­
ants to necroptosis111.

Notably, both RIPK1–/– human Jurkat lymphocytes 
and cPLA2-deficient murine L929 cells fail to accumu­

deletion of β2 integrin mimic LAD‑I more accurately44.

animals that carry a complete 
deletion of β2 integrin have deficiencies in T cell acti­
vation44,45 or extravasation46, and also display aberrant 
B cell differentiation that results from an increase in 
interleukin‑6 (IL‑6) production47.

experiment.system: mouse models of β2 integrin (CD18) hypomorph and null
experiment.perturbation: genetic hypomorphic allele or complete deletion of β2 integrin; chemically induced peritonitis
experiment.measurement: inflammatory response, skin inflammation, T cell activation/extravasation, B cell differentiation and IL-6

text: In the absence of β2 integrin, fewer neutrophils are present in the wound and macrophages can no longer engulf cells or secrete TGFβ, a defective cascade the authors present as explaining prolonged healing times and as showing that adhesome mutations have consequences beyond cell-autonomous adhesion and signalling defects.

quotes.quote:
In the absence of 
β2 integrin, not only are there fewer neutrophils present 
in the wound, but macrophages can no longer engulf 
cells or secrete TGFβ51. This defective signalling cas­
cade, which leads to prolonged healing times, illustrates 
that mutating components of the adhesome can have 
consequences beyond cell autonomous adhesion and 
signallin­g defects.

experiment.system: β2 integrin-deficient mice and patients with LAD-I
experiment.perturbation: loss of β2 integrin
experiment.measurement: neutrophil numbers at wound, macrophage engulfment and TGFβ secretion, wound healing time

text: Deletion of α7 integrin in mice produces a muscular dystrophy phenotype with centrally located nuclei, variable fibre size and myotendinous junction detachment, plus vascular smooth muscle defects not reported in humans, and α5 integrin expression persists into adulthood; no heart defects have been reported in knockout mice or in humans with α7 integrin gene mutations.

quotes.quote:
deletion of α7 integrin in mice leads to a mus­
cular dystrophy phenotype66,67, in addition to vascular 
smooth muscle defects that have not been reported in 
humans68

dele­
tion of α7 integrin causes muscle degeneration that is 
characterized by centrally located nuclei and variable 
fibre size66. Detachment from the m­yotendinous junctio­n 
is also apparent

in mice that lack 
α7 integrin, the expression of α5 integrin, which is nor­
mally only expressed in embryonic muscle, persists into 
adulthood67

no defects in heart structure or function have 
been reported in knockout mice or humans with muta­
tions in the gene encoding α7 integrin

experiment.system: α7 integrin knockout mice; humans with α7 integrin mutation
experiment.perturbation: genetic deletion of α7 integrin
experiment.measurement: muscle histology, myotendinous junction integrity, integrin expression, cardiac structure/function

text: Vinculin perturbation in mice models human cardiomyopathy: constitutive VCL deletion is embryonic lethal, mice with a single Vcl allele show ultrastructural defects and develop cardiomyopathy under increased haemodynamic load, and cardiac-specific VCL deletion produces dilated cardiomyopathy with dissolution of intercalated discs; skeletal muscle weakness has not been reported in patients or mice with VCL mutations.

quotes.quote:
Although constitutive deletion of VCL is embryonic 
lethal76, mice that express a single Vcl allele showed 
ultrastructural defects and developed cardiomyopathy in 
response to increased haemodynamic load77. Mice that 
express a cardiac-specific deletion of VCL developed 
DCM, which is characterized by the dissolution of inter­
calated discs78. Interestingly, skeletal muscle weaknes­s 
has not been reported in patients or mice with VCL 
mutations, which implies a specific cardiac phenotype.

experiment.system: vinculin (VCL) mutant mice and patients with metavinculin/vinculin mutations
experiment.perturbation: constitutive, heterozygous or cardiac-specific deletion of VCL; increased haemodynamic load
experiment.measurement: viability, cardiac ultrastructure and cardiomyopathy phenotype

text: Constitutive LDB3 deletion in mice causes severe myopathy, cardiac-specific ablation leads to severe dilated cardiomyopathy and premature death before 23 weeks of age, and mice carrying the patient-relevant Ldb3 point mutation S196L develop DCM at a slower rate.

quotes.quote:
Mice in which 
LDB3 is constitutively deleted exhibit severe myopathy, 
which confirms the role of this protein in muscle func­
tion83. A cardiac-specific ablation of LDB3 in mice leads 
to severe DCM and premature death before 23 weeks 
of age84; conversely, mice that express a patient-relevant 
point mutation in Ldb3 (S196L) develop DCM at a 
slower rate

experiment.system: LDB3 (cypher/ZASP) mutant mice
experiment.perturbation: constitutive deletion, cardiac-specific ablation, or S196L point mutation of Ldb3
experiment.measurement: myopathy severity, DCM onset rate, survival

numbers.quantity: premature death age after cardiac-specific LDB3 ablation

text: Complete ablation of the β4 or α6 integrin subunit in mice causes perinatal lethality with severe skin blistering reminiscent of extreme JEB, whereas conditional inducible α6 deletion in epidermis is tolerated but produces blistering, alopecia, inflammation and keratinocyte hyperproliferation, and mosaic β4 deletion produces blistering and inflammation where it is absent.

quotes.quote:
Complete ablation 
of the β4 or α6 subunit in mice leads to perinatal lethal­
ity with severe skin blistering, which is reminiscent of 
extreme cases of JEB88–90. Conditional, inducible deletion 
of α6 integrin from the mouse epidermis is tolerated, 
although it produces blistering, alopecia, inflamma­
tion and hyperproliferation of keratinocytes as seen 
in patients with JEB91,92; mosaic deletion of β4 integrin 
results in blistering and inflammation in areas where it 
is absent93.

experiment.system: mouse models of α6 and β4 integrin loss; JEB patients
experiment.perturbation: complete, conditional inducible or mosaic genetic deletion of α6 or β4 integrin
experiment.measurement: survival, skin blistering, inflammation, keratinocyte proliferation

text: Homozygous α3 integrin gene mutations were identified in three patients with nephrotic syndrome, pulmonary disease and skin fragility who died during infancy, matching α3-null mouse lung and kidney malformations and skin blistering; basement membrane deposits on both sides of blisters suggest a role for α3 integrin in assembling and remodelling the basement membrane rather than anchoring cells.

quotes.quote:
Homozygous mutations in the gene encoding α3 inte­
grin have been identified in three patients with nephrotic 
syndrome, pulmonary disease and skin fragility, which 
resulted in death during infancy94,95.

blisters 
from mice and patients contain basement membrane 
deposits on both the dermal and epidermal sides of the 
bliste­r, which suggests a role for α3 integrin in assem­
bling and remodelling the basement membrane, rather 
than in anchoring cells to it

experiment.system: patients with homozygous ITGA3 mutations; α3 subunit-deficient mice
experiment.perturbation: loss-of-function mutation/deletion of α3 integrin
experiment.measurement: kidney, lung and skin phenotypes; basement membrane deposits in blisters

numbers.quantity: patients with homozygous α3 integrin mutations

text: Increased ILK and FAK expression is detected in human cardiac hypertrophy biopsies; cardiomyocyte-specific transgenic ILK overexpression in mice phenocopies the human disease and siRNA-mediated reduction of FAK in vivo attenuates hypertrophy in a mouse volume-overload model.

quotes.quote:
In human biopsy samples, increased 
expression of integrin-linked kinase (ILK) and focal 
adhesion kinase (FAK) has been detected124,125. These 
molecules probably directly contribute to hypertrophy, 
as cardiomyocyte-specific transgenic overexpression of 
ILK in mice phenocopies the human disease124, and a 
siRNA-mediated reduction in FAK expression in vivo 
attenuates hypertrophy in a mouse model of volume 
overload126.

experiment.system: human cardiac hypertrophy biopsies; transgenic and siRNA-treated mice
experiment.perturbation: cardiomyocyte-specific ILK overexpression; siRNA knockdown of FAK; volume overload
experiment.measurement: ILK/FAK expression and hypertrophy phenotype

text: Two FAK-deletion studies in cardiomyocytes gave opposite results — one showed prevention of hypertrophy, the other promotion — and the authors note the discrepancy may relate to the age at maximal FAK deletion (FAK detectable for three months in the protective study versus undetectable two weeks after birth in the promoting study).

quotes.quote:
one study demonstrated that the deletion 
of FAK in cardiomyocytes prevents hypertrophy130, 
whereas another study showed that hypertrophy was 
promoted in the absence of FAK131. One reason behind 
the discrepancy may be the age of the organism at which 
maximal FAK deletion was detected. In the study in 
which loss of FAK was protective, FAK remained 
detectable for three months, whereas in the study in 
which FAK loss promoted hypertrophy, FAK protein 
was undetectable two weeks after birth.

experiment.system: mouse cardiomyocyte FAK-deletion models
experiment.perturbation: genetic deletion of FAK in cardiomyocytes
experiment.measurement: cardiac hypertrophy phenotype and timing of FAK protein loss

numbers.quantity: time FAK undetectable in promoting study

text: Mouse models show that disrupting the balance of RHO GTPase activity leads to actin cytoskeletal changes and FSGS, and a mutation in the adhesome-associated RACGAP gene ARHGAP24 was identified in humans, establishing RHO GTPase dysregulation as an important mediator of FSGS.

quotes.quote:
Mouse models showed that disrupting the balance of 
RHO GTPase activity leads to changes in the actin 
cytoskeleton and establishment of FSGS in mice132,133. 
Recently, a mutation in an adhesome-associated 
RACGAP gene, ARHGAP24 (encoding RHOGAP24; 
also known as FILGAP and p73RHOGAP), was identified 
in humans, establishing RHO GTPase dysregulation as 
an important mediator of FSGS133.

experiment.system: mouse podocytes/kidney; human FSGS patients
experiment.perturbation: genetic disruption of RHO GTPase balance in mice; ARHGAP24 mutation in humans
experiment.measurement: actin cytoskeleton changes and FSGS phenotype

text: Biopsies from FSGS patients show increased ILK expression and cultured podocytes show increased ILK-related activity when exposed to plasma from FSGS patients, which the authors relate to the 20–30% rate of recurrent FSGS in kidney transplant recipients.

quotes.quote:
Biopsy material from patients with FSGS 
show increased ILK expression137, and cultured podo­
cytes show an increase in ILK-related activity when 
they are exposed to plasma from patients with FSGS138. 
This intriguing finding may help to explain the high 
rate of recurrent FSGS (20–30%) in patients that receive 
kidney transplants139.

experiment.system: FSGS patient biopsies and cultured podocytes
experiment.perturbation: exposure of cultured podocytes to plasma from patients with FSGS
experiment.measurement: ILK expression and ILK-related activity; recurrence rate after transplantation

numbers.quantity: recurrent FSGS rate after kidney transplant

text: Integrins containing αv subunits account for 50% of described virus–integrin interactions, and although αvβ3 integrin recognizes RGD-containing ligands, some viruses bind this integrin in the absence of an RGD sequence.

quotes.quote:
Integrins that contain αv subunits seem to 
be favoured by many viruses, accounting for 50% of 
described virus–integrin interactions, and whereas 
αvβ3 integrin recognizes RGD (Arg-Gly-Asp)-
containing ligands, some viruses can bind to this inte­
grin in the absence of an RGD sequence142–144.

experiment.system: catalogued virus–integrin interactions (Supplementary tables)
experiment.perturbation: observational; literature survey of virus–integrin binding
experiment.measurement: proportion of interactions involving αv-containing integrins and RGD dependence

numbers.quantity: share of virus–integrin interactions involving αv integrins

text: For HCMV, αvβ3 integrin functions as a co-receptor with EGFR to promote viral uptake in a PI3K- and SRC-dependent manner, and adenovirus requires αvβ3 and αvβ5 integrins as co-receptors for entry via RAC1-mediated actin reorganization downstream of PI3K, though neither integrin is required for cell attachment.

quotes.quote:
In the case of human 
cytomegalo­virus (HCMV), αvβ3 integrin functions 
as a co‑receptor, together with epidermal growth fac­
tor receptor (EGFR), to promote viral uptake by a 
mechanism dependent on PI3K and SRC activity148. 
Likewise, adenovirus requires the involvement of 
αvβ3 and αvβ5 integrins to facilitate cell entry through 
RAC1‑mediated reorganization of the actin cytoskel­
eton downstream of PI3K, but neither of these integrins 
is required for cell attachment

experiment.system: cultured cells infected with HCMV or adenovirus
experiment.perturbation: integrin/EGFR engagement; inhibition of PI3K, SRC, RAC1 pathways
experiment.measurement: viral attachment vs internalization

text: In contrast to viruses, bacteria show a marked preference for interacting with hosts through β1 integrins; the authors suggest this may reflect increased resistance to force of β1 integrins compared with β3 integrins.

quotes.quote:
In contrast to viruses, bacteria 
show a marked preference for interacting with their 
hosts through β1 integrins. The reasons for this are 
unclear, but may be due to the increased resistance to 
force that β1 integrins exhibit as compared to β3 inte­
grins, which may be important for bacterial uptake155.

experiment.system: bacteria–host cell interactions catalogued from literature
experiment.perturbation: observational; survey of bacterial integrin usage
experiment.measurement: integrin subtype preference in bacterial attachment/uptake

text: Binding of Staphylococcus aureus to α5β1 integrin stimulates cytosolic assembly of a fibrillar adhesion-like adhesion and internalization in a FAK- and cortactin-dependent process, with similar FAK–SRC and cortactin involvement seen in Neisseria meningitidis and Shigella spp. invasion.

quotes.quote:
The bind­
ing of Staphylococcus aureus to α5β1 integrin stimu­
lates the cytosolic assembly of a fibrillar adhesion-like 
adhesion, and subsequently the internalization of this 
bacterium in a FAK- and cortactin-dependent pro­
cess156.

Similar involvement of FAK–SRC signal­
ling and cortactin has been observed in the invasion of 
Neisseria meningitidis158 and Shigella spp.159.

experiment.system: host cells infected with S. aureus, N. meningitidis or Shigella
experiment.perturbation: bacterial binding to α5β1 integrin; interference with FAK/SRC/cortactin
experiment.measurement: adhesion assembly and bacterial internalization

text: Combined gene knockout, siRNA knockdown and dominant-negative expression revealed that β1 integrin-mediated attachment of Campylobacter jejuni activates FAK, leading to activation of the RAC GEFs DOCK1 and TIAM1 and RAC-mediated actin rearrangements; separately, downregulation of ILK expression or activity impairs invasion by S. pyogenes, S. aureus and Yersinia spp.

quotes.quote:
A combination of gene knockout, siRNA knock­
down and dominant-negative gene expression has ena­
bled the dissection of the molecular mechanism that 
underlies Campylobacter jejuni cell invasion. It was 
revealed that β1 integrin‑mediated cell attachment 
causes the activation of FAK, which leads to the activa­
tion of the RAC GEFs dedicator of cytokinesis protein 1 
(DOCK1, also known as DOCK180) and T lymphoma 
invasion and metastasis-inducing 1 (TIAM1), and 
subsequently RAC-mediated actin rearrangements160.

downregulation of ILK expression or activ­
ity was shown to impair the invasion of Staphylococcus 
pyogenes, S. aureus and Yersinia spp.161.

experiment.system: host epithelial cells infected with C. jejuni or other bacteria
experiment.perturbation: gene knockout, siRNA knockdown, dominant-negative expression; ILK downregulation
experiment.measurement: bacterial invasion and signalling pathway activation

text: The Shigella virulence factor OspE binds ILK and stabilizes its membrane association; the OspE–ILK complex increased surface expression and activation of β1 integrin, which reduces cell detachment, and the authors note OspE is conserved across many pathogenic bacteria.

quotes.quote:
Intracellular 
Shigella spp. secrete a virulence factor, outer surface pro­
tein E (OspE), which has recently been shown to bind 
ILK and to stabilize its association with the cell mem­
brane162. The OspE–ILK complex increased the surface 
expression and activation of β1 integrin, which reduces 
cell detachment. As OspE is conserved across many 
pathogenic bacteria, blocking epithelial exfoliation by 
strengthening cell adhesion may be a general mechanism­ 
by which many bacteria evade this host defence.

experiment.system: epithelial cells infected with Shigella
experiment.perturbation: bacterial secretion of OspE binding ILK
experiment.measurement: ILK membrane association, β1 integrin surface expression/activation, cell detachment

text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae binding to CEACAMs increases expression of CD105 (endoglin), which sequesters zyxin away from integrin attachments where CD105 acts as a negative regulator of adhesion, thereby increasing integrin activation.

quotes.quote: Through binding carcino­

(CEACAMs) they increase the expression of cluster 
of differentiation 105 (CD105; also known as endog­
lin), a member of the TGFβ1 receptor family163. CD105 
sequesters zyxin away from integrin attachments, 
in which CD105 functions as a negative regulator of 
adhesio­n, thus increasing integrin activation164,165.

experiment.system: epithelial cells infected with Neisseria gonorrhoeae
experiment.perturbation: bacterial engagement of CEACAMs
experiment.measurement: CD105 expression, zyxin localization, integrin activation and epithelial shedding

text: Five integrin-targeting drugs are currently applied in the clinic (natalizumab, efalizumab, abciximab, eptifibatide and tirofiban), with natalizumab and efalizumab linked to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy leading to efalizumab's withdrawal in 2009 and natalizumab's temporary withdrawal before reapproval in 2010.

quotes.quote:
Currently, five 
integrin targeting drugs have been applied in the clinic166.

Natalizumab and efalizumab have been 
linked to occurrences of progressive multi­focal leuko­
encephalopathy (PML), an opportunistic viral infection. 
As a result, efalizumab was withdrawn from the market 
in 2009 and natalizumab was withdrawn temporarily 
before its use was reapproved in 2010.

experiment.system: clinically approved integrin-targeting drugs
experiment.perturbation: observational; survey of clinical integrin antagonists and their regulatory history
experiment.measurement: number of approved drugs, targets, indications and adverse events

text: At least 260 additional integrin-targeting compounds are in clinical trials, among them vedolizumab (anti-α4β7, not shown to cause PML to date) and cilengitide, a small molecule targeting αv integrins in a Phase III trial for glioblastoma and Phase II trials for other cancers.

quotes.quote:
there are at least 260 additional compounds currently in 
clinical trials166. Among the most promising of these are 
vedolizumab (Entyvio; Millennium Pharmaceuticals), 
an antibody against α4β7 integrin that to date has not 
been shown to cause PML

cilengitide (Impetreve; Merck), a 
small-molecule that targets αv integrins and is currently 
in a Phase III clinical trial for glioblastoma treatment 
and in Phase II trials for other cancers172.

experiment.system: integrin-targeting compounds in clinical development
experiment.perturbation: observational; survey of clinical trial pipeline
experiment.measurement: number of compounds in trials and their targets/phases

text: Live-cell imaging has visualized gradients rather than a uniform intracellular distribution of cAMP, indicating accumulation at specific sites, in contrast to the earlier view of free diffusion with a theoretical range-of-action of 220 µm.

quotes.quote:
cAMP was initially considered to be a second mes-
senger that diffused freely throughout the cell with a
theoretical range-of-action of 220 µm (REF. 5).
However, advances in live-cell imaging have visualized
gradients, rather than a uniform intracellular distribu-
tion, of cAMP, which indicates that this second mes-
senger accumulates at specific sites within cells

experiment.system: living cells
experiment.perturbation: observational
experiment.measurement: live-cell imaging of intracellular cAMP distribution

text: AKAPs contain an amphipathic helix of 14–18 residues that binds the N-terminal dimerization domain of the PKA R subunit; NMR solution structure shows the hydrophobic face of the helix lying across the four-helix bundle formed by the R-subunit dimer.

quotes.quote:
AKAPs contain an amphi-
pathic helix of 14–18 residues,which binds to the N-ter-
minal dimerization domain of the R subunit of
PKA21–23. The NMR solution structure of such a com-
plex has revealed that the hydrophobic face of the AKAP
amphipathic helix lies across the four-helix bundle that
is formed by the R-subunit dimer

experiment.system: AKAP amphipathic helix–PKA R-subunit dimer complex
experiment.perturbation: observational (structural)
experiment.measurement: NMR solution structure and binding

text: Bioinformatic design produced a 17-residue peptide, AKAP-IS, that binds RII with greater affinity than Ht31 and disrupts PKA anchoring inside cells; a separately prepared RI-selective antagonist shows a 100-fold preference for RI over RII.

quotes.quote:
Bioinformatic design of an optimal RII-anchoring
antagonist has generated a 17-residue peptide that is
known as AKAP-IS, which binds to RII with greater
affinity than Ht31 and can disrupt PKA anchoring
inside cells29.An RI-selective anchoring antagonist has
also been prepared that shows a 100-fold preference for
RI over RII (REF. 30).

experiment.system: PKA R subunits and cells
experiment.perturbation: designed peptide antagonists (AKAP-IS, RI-selective peptide) versus Ht31
experiment.measurement: binding affinity for RII/RI and disruption of PKA anchoring in cells

text: AKAP79 was shown by yeast two-hybrid assay to interact with the A subunit of the Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase PP2B in 1995, and PKC was found one year later to be a component of the AKAP79/150 complex, making it a locus for simultaneous anchoring of PKA, PP2B and PKC.

quotes.quote:
In 1995,AKAP79 was shown by yeast two-
hybrid assay to interact with the A subunit of the
Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase PP2B45. One
year later, protein kinase C (PKC) was also found to be

a component of the AKAP79/150 signalling complex46.
At that time, the simultaneous anchoring of these three
signalling enzymes — PKA, PP2B and PKC — was
thought to generate a locus for the integration of
distinct second-messenger signals at postsynaptic
membranes

experiment.system: AKAP79/150 protein complexes
experiment.perturbation: observational (yeast two-hybrid interaction assay)
experiment.measurement: protein–protein interaction / complex composition

text: WAVE1 assembles different complexes in different tissues: at the cytoskeleton it binds PKA, Abl, Rac, WRP and the Arp2/3 complex, whereas a proteomic approach using liver tissue isolated WAVE1 in a mitochondrial complex containing PKA, PP1, BAD and glucokinase; Bad-null mice are deficient in glucose homeostasis.

quotes.quote:
A
different proteomic approach using liver tissue has iso-
lated WAVE1 as part of a mitochondrial complex that
contains PKA, the type-1 protein phosphatase PP1, the
pro-apoptotic protein BAD and the metabolic enzyme
glucokinase36

Furthermore, Bad-null mice are deficient in glu-
cose homeostasis,which is consistent with the presence
of glucokinase in the complex36

experiment.system: mouse liver tissue and Bad-null mice
experiment.perturbation: proteomic purification of WAVE1 complexes; Bad gene knockout
experiment.measurement: complex composition; glucose homeostasis

text: The phenotype of WAVE1-knockout mice suggests that a direct link between WAVE1 and WRP is functionally important for sensorimotor and cognate behaviours.

quotes.quote:
the
phenotype of WAVE1-knockout mice suggests that a
direct link between WAVE1 and WRP is functionally
important for sensorimotor and cognate behaviours68

experiment.system: WAVE1-knockout mice
experiment.perturbation: WAVE1 gene knockout
experiment.measurement: sensorimotor and cognate behaviours

text: In a postsynaptic AKAP79/150 complex attached indirectly to the GluR1 subunit of the AMPA receptor via PSD-95 or SAP97, anchored PKA promotes basal phosphorylation of GluR1 on Ser845 while anchored PP2B dephosphorylates GluR1 at this site and causes downregulation of the current.

quotes.quote:
a postsynaptic AKAP79/150 signalling com-
plex that consists of PKA and PP2B is attached indi-
rectly to the GluR1 subunit of the AMPA receptor77.
Functional studies indicate that anchored PKA pro-
motes basal phosphorylation of GluR1 on Ser845,
whereas anchored PP2B dephosphorylates GluR1 at
this site and causes downregulation of the current78.

experiment.system: neuronal postsynaptic AKAP79/150–AMPA receptor complexes
experiment.perturbation: anchored PKA/PP2B activity (functional studies)
experiment.measurement: GluR1 Ser845 phosphorylation and AMPA-receptor current

text: AKAP-anchored PP2B may dephosphorylate and activate the PSD-95-associated ubiquitin E3 ligase MDM2, leading to PSD-95 ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation, breaking the channel–AKAP79/150 link and triggering AMPA receptor internalization.

quotes.quote:
Recent studies indicate that AKAP-anchored PP2B
might dephosphorylate and thereby activate a PSD-95-
associated UBIQUITIN E3 LIGASE, mouse double minute-2
(MDM2)85. As a result, PSD-95 is ubiquitylated and
removed by proteasomal degradation, the link
between the channel and AKAP79/150 is broken, and
the internalization of AMPA receptors is triggered85

experiment.system: neuronal postsynaptic PSD-95/AKAP79/150/AMPA receptor complexes
experiment.perturbation: anchored PP2B-mediated MDM2 activation
experiment.measurement: PSD-95 ubiquitylation/degradation and AMPA receptor surface expression

text: Electrophysiological studies show the KCNQ2 channel binds directly to AKAP79/150, which anchors PKC to phosphorylate Ser541 on the channel as the basis for muscarinic M-current inhibition; experiments with mutant anchoring proteins indicate PKA-anchoring sequences are not required for this modulation.

quotes.quote:
Recent electrophysiological studies show that a
core component of the M current,the KCNQ2 channel,
binds directly to AKAP79/150 (REF. 93)

sites at which it can efficiently phosphorylate Ser541 on
the channel,which is the molecular basis for M-current
inhibition by muscarinic agonists94 (FIG.4d).Furthermore,
biochemical and electrophysiological experiments using
mutant forms of the anchoring protein have indicated
that PKA-anchoring sequences are not required for the
modulation of KCNQ2 channels by AKAP79/150-
bound PKC94.

experiment.system: neurons/cells expressing KCNQ2 channels and AKAP79/150
experiment.perturbation: muscarinic agonist stimulation; mutant AKAP79/150 lacking PKA-anchoring sequences
experiment.measurement: M-current electrophysiology and channel phosphorylation

text: In cardiomyocytes mAKAP synchronizes PKA and PDE4D3; activated PKA phosphorylates PDE4D3 on Ser54 to increase the VMAX of the enzyme 2–3 fold over basal conditions, forming a negative-feedback loop (the figure legend states phosphorylation of Ser54 increases phosphodiesterase activity twofold).

quotes.quote:
This anchoring
protein synchronizes the activities of PKA and a cAMP-
specific phosphodiesterase,PDE4D3,in cardiomyocytes97.

The newly activated PKA
phosphorylates PDE4D3 on Ser54 to increase the VMAXof
the enzyme 2–3 fold over basal conditions10,98,99.

Phosphorylation of Ser54
increases the activity of the phosphodiesterase twofold10,98,99

experiment.system: mAKAP–PKA–PDE4D3 complex in cardiomyocytes
experiment.perturbation: hormonal stimulation raising cAMP / PKA phosphorylation of PDE4D3 Ser54
experiment.measurement: phosphodiesterase VMAX/activity relative to basal

numbers.quantity: fold increase in PDE4D3 VMAX after Ser54 phosphorylation
fold increase in phosphodiesterase activity (figure legend)

text: PKA-mediated phosphorylation of Ser1565 of AKAP-Lbc is required to recruit 14-3-3, and cellular studies show 14-3-3 binding inhibits the Rho-GEF activity of AKAP-Lbc, an effect accentuated by activation of PKA.

quotes.quote:
Two
groups have independently shown that PKA-mediated
phosphorylation of Ser1565 of AKAP-Lbc is required to
recruit 14-3-3 to the anchoring protein101,102 (FIG. 6a,b).
Cellular studies show that 14-3-3 binding inhibits the
Rho-GEF activity of AKAP-Lbc (FIG.6c),an effect that is
accentuated by activation of PKA.

experiment.system: cells expressing AKAP-Lbc
experiment.perturbation: PKA activation and Ser1565 phosphorylation-dependent 14-3-3 recruitment
experiment.measurement: 14-3-3 binding and Rho-GEF activity

text: PKA phosphorylation of PDE4D3 on Ser13, within its mAKAP-binding domain, increases its affinity for mAKAP in vitro; cellular experiments show PKA activation enhances the mAKAP–PDE4D3 interaction, while disrupting mAKAP's ability to anchor PKA diminishes it.

quotes.quote:
Ser13 (REF. 104). This residue lies within the mAKAP-
binding domain97 and in vitro binding studies show that
phosphorylation of this residue increases the affinity of
PDE4D3 for the anchoring protein105. Cellular experi-
ments show that activation of PKA enhances the
mAKAP–PDE4D3 interaction. This is further con-
firmed using phospho-mutants of PDE4D3 that mimic
the unphosphorylated and phosphorylated Ser13,
whereas disruption of the ability of mAKAP to anchor
PKA diminishes the AKAP–PDE4D3 interaction105.

experiment.system: mAKAP–PDE4D3 complex, in vitro and in cells
experiment.perturbation: PKA activation; Ser13 phospho-mimetic mutants; disruption of PKA anchoring on mAKAP
experiment.measurement: PDE4D3 binding affinity for mAKAP

text: AKAP-Lbc nucleates a PKD activation cascade: it recruits the upstream kinase PKCη near PKD, and PKA-mediated phosphorylation of AKAP-Lbc at Ser2737 within the PKD-binding domain releases the newly activated PKD into the cytoplasm.

quotes.quote:
First,it recruits the upstream activating kinase PKCη109
and orients it in close proximity to PKD.

Second,AKAP-Lbc directs PKA-mediated phosphoryla-
tion of the anchoring protein itself at a Ser residue within
the PKD binding domain (Ser2737),which releases the
newly activated PKD enzyme into the cytoplasm (FIG.7b).

experiment.system: AKAP-Lbc kinase-scaffold complex in cells
experiment.perturbation: PKA-mediated phosphorylation of AKAP-Lbc Ser2737
experiment.measurement: PKD activation and release from the anchoring protein

text: Gravin targets PKA and PKC to the neuromuscular junction or membrane cytoskeleton and is dynamically recruited to β2-AR: agonist stimulation initially strengthens gravin–β2-AR association through PKA phosphorylation of Ser696, Ser698 and Ser772, while prolonged stimulation triggers PKC phosphorylation, β-arrestin-dependent MDM2 recruitment, ubiquitylation, proteasomal degradation and receptor trafficking.

quotes.quote:
Agonist stimu-
lation initially strengthens the association of gravin with
the β2-AR65,117 through PKA-mediated phosphorylation
of Ser696,Ser698 and Ser772 on the anchoring protein
(FIG.8a).However,prolonged agonist stimulation also sets
into motion a sequence of events that dismantles the
signalling complex. This includes phosphorylation by
PKC,ubiquitylation,proteasomal degradation and β2-AR
trafficking117,119

A key molecule in this downregu-
lation process is the regulatory adaptor protein β-arrestin,

text: A gene's network coverage (number of interactomes containing it) correlated strongly with its citation count (rs,citation = 0.80, p = 1 × 10−50); the relationship was diminished but not eliminated among experimental networks only (rs = 0.48, p = 1 × 10−50), and mRNA expression (rs,mRNA = 0.59) and protein abundance (rs,protein = 0.40) also correlated significantly with coverage. the
smaller
PCNet2.1
(top
8
interactomes,

interactions), and for a CC-free alternative, we deﬁned PCNet2.2

experiment.perturbation: selection of thresholds balancing performance and parsimony (PCNet2.1 additionally restricted to a maximum of two million interactions)
experiment.measurement: interaction counts and mean centralized rank across Literature and Genetic gene sets

text: In interaction prediction, precision was higher for held-out interactions than external interactions and MPS generally outperformed L3; DIP and Reactome had the highest held-out precision (P@k via MPS of 0.57 and 0.55), Havugimana (P@k = 0.21, L3) and PTMCode2 (P@k = 0.16, MPS) led for CORUM complex interactions, and SIGNOR (P@k = 0.05, L3) and Reactome (P@k = 0.04, L3) performed best for PANTHER pathway interactions.

quotes.quote:
Across all inter-
actomes, prediction precision was higher for held-out interactions
than external interactions, and MPS generally produced stronger
predictions than L3 (Fig. 5A–C). DIP (Xenarios et al, 2000) and
Reactome (Gillespie et al, 2022) showed the highest precision for
the held-out task, predicting interactions with average precisions at
k (P@k) via MPS of 0.57 and 0.55, respectively (Fig. 5A). For
CORUM interactions, networks such as Havugimana (Havugi-
mana et al, 2012) (P@k = 0.21, L3) and PTMCode2 (Minguez et al,
2015) (P@k = 0.16, MPS) led in precision (Fig. 5B). In contrast,
curated interactomes such as SIGNOR (Lo Surdo et al, 2022)
(P@k = 0.05, L3) and Reactome (P@k = 0.04, L3) showed the best
performance
for
predicting
PANTHER
pathway
interactions

experiment.system: panel of interactomes (excluding those with prohibitive computational cost or resource circularity)
experiment.perturbation: interaction prediction with L3 and MPS algorithms; 10-fold cross-validation holding out 10% of edges; evaluation against external CORUM complex and PANTHER pathway interaction sets
experiment.measurement: precision at k (P@k) with k = size of test set

text: Smaller interactomes tended to predict high-quality interactions, as evidenced by broad support from other networks; while all interactomes shared some interactions with the CORUM and PANTHER sets, the extent of this overlap did not drive predictive performance for these external interaction sets.

quotes.quote: We further observed that smaller interactomes tended

to predict high-quality interactions, as evidenced by broad support
from other networks (Fig. 5D). While all interactomes shared some
interactions with the CORUM and PANTHER sets (Fig. EV4A,B),
the extent of this overlap did not drive predictive performance for
these external interaction sets (Fig. EV4C,D).

experiment.system: top 100 interactions predicted by each interactome via MPS and L3
experiment.perturbation: interaction prediction from full interactomes
experiment.measurement: network coverage distribution of top predictions across the 45 interactomes; percent overlap of CORUM/PANTHER sets with each interactome versus predictive performance

text: Hierarchical decomposition with HiDeF showed ConsensusPathDB, FunCoup, PROPER, TFLink, and hu.MAP identified many small assemblies while STRING, HumanNet, and Pathway Commons identified larger assemblies; DIP and Havugimana captured the most CORUM complexes, PrePPI and SIGNOR gave the highest GO annotation similarity among complex members, GeneMANIA, STRING, and HumanNet had the highest mean clustering coefficient, and Reactome and ReactomeFI were consistently among the top across all three metrics.

quotes.quote:
Networks such as ConsensusPathDB (Kamburov et al, 2008),
FunCoup (Persson et al, 2021), PROPER (Johnson et al, 2021),
TFLink (Liska et al, 2022), and hu.MAP (Drew et al, 2021)
identiﬁed a large number of small assemblies, while others, such as
STRING (Szklarczyk et al, 2023), HumanNet (Kim et al, 2022), and
Pathway Commons (Rodchenkov et al, 2020), tended to identify

larger assemblies (Fig. EV4E). Interactomes such as DIP (Xenarios
et al, 2000) and Havugimana (Havugimana et al, 2012) captured the
greatest number of CORUM complexes (Fig. EV4F), while PrePPI
(Petrey et al, 2023) and SIGNOR (Lo Surdo et al, 2022) identiﬁed
complexes with the highest GO annotation similarities among
complex members (Fig. EV4G).

we also
examined the mean clustering coefﬁcient of predicted complexes,
observing the highest clustering for GeneMANIA (Mostafavi et al,
2008), STRING (Szklarczyk et al, 2023), and HumanNet (Kim et al,
2022)
(Fig.
EV4H). Reactome
(Gillespie
et
al,
2022)
and
ReactomeFI (preprint: Brunson et al, 2023) were consistently
among the top-performing interactomes across all three metrics.

experiment.system: hierarchical community structures of each interactome
experiment.perturbation: HiDeF hierarchical community decoding at maximum resolution 10
experiment.measurement: number/size of assemblies, CORUM complexes recovered at Jaccard ≥ 0.5, GO semantic similarity score, and mean clustering coefficient

text: AlphaFold-Multimer modeling of randomly sampled reported interactions gave higher ipTM scores for interactions present in more than 25 interactomes, especially for the most supported interactions (≥33 supporting interactomes), a pattern consistent with higher proportions of experimentally resolved structures among highly supported interactions; nine interactomes contained interactions with significantly higher ipTM scores than randomly generated protein pairs (q < 0.15), with PDB structures generally accounting for fewer than 20% of tested interactions.

quotes.quote:
Applying AlphaFold-Multimer (AF) to random selec-
tions of interactions with varying network coverage, we observed

higher interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) scores for
interactions present in more than 25 interactomes (Fig. 5E),
especially for the most supported interactions (≥33 supporting
interactomes). This pattern was consistent with higher proportions
of experimentally resolved structures amongst highly supported
interactions (Appendix Fig. S3A). We further identiﬁed nine
interactomes containing interactions with signiﬁcantly higher
ipTM scores than randomly generated protein pairs (Fig. 5F,
q < 0.15). Again, we observed a correlation between the presence of
experimentally resolved structures in PDB and ipTM scores,
though these generally accounted for fewer than 20% of tested
interactions

experiment.system: samples of 50 reported interactions per network coverage value and per interactome, modeled with ColabFold/AlphaFold-Multimer
experiment.perturbation: comparison to a background distribution of 1779 randomly generated protein pairs
experiment.measurement: interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) score; two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test with BH correction

numbers.quantity: coverage threshold above which ipTM increases
share of tested interactions with resolved structures

text: Interactome rankings for interaction prediction varied substantially from rankings for gene set recovery, and unlike gene set recovery the precision of interaction prediction was not driven by interactome size; top interaction-prediction networks included many with improved size-adjusted gene set recovery performance, and after size adjustment HumanNet and DIP had the highest gene set recovery performance per interaction.

quotes.quote:
In contrast to gene set recovery results, the precision of
interaction prediction was not driven by interactome size, and overall
interactome rankings for interaction prediction varied substantially
from rankings for gene set recovery (Fig. 5A–C, Table 1). In particular,
the top-performing networks included many with improved size-
adjusted performance in gene set recovery, indicating the quality
rather than quantity of interactions is crucial for interaction
prediction.

After
adjusting for this size effect, we found that HumanNet (Kim et al,
2022) and DIP (Xenarios et al, 2000) had the highest performance
per interaction

experiment.system: 45 interactomes evaluated by both gene set recovery and interaction prediction
experiment.perturbation: regression-based size adjustment on log10 interaction count
experiment.measurement: comparison of centralized performance ranks and P@k across tasks

text: Comparing gene citation counts with interactome coverage, the authors report Spearman correlations for protein-coding genes, and also compare network coverage to mean mRNA expression in GTEx and mean protein abundance in the Human Protein Atlas, with Spearman correlations reported for each.

quotes.quote: (B) Comparison of network coverage and NCBI gene citation count as of December 20, 2023, for genes that are protein-coding or present in at least one interactome. Genes with no reported citations are excluded. Spearman correlation reported for protein-coding genes.

(D, E) Network coverage of protein-coding genes as a function of mean mRNA expression across all tissues in GTEx (D) and mean protein abundance across all tissues in the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) (E).

Original citation counts (“Raw”), and citation counts adjusted for mean gene mRNA expression using log–log ordinary least squares regression (“Adjusted”). Spearman correlations reported.

Genes were ﬁltered to those with non-zero expression in a maximum of two tissues (1400/1740 genes). Tissues with at least one reported interaction amongst the ﬁltered genes are shown and clustered by minimum distance.

text: Gene set recovery statistics were computed for 45 interactomes, with network coverage defined as the number of networks containing at least 20 set genes and each gene set's AUPRC, Performance, and Performance Gain taken as the median across networks containing at least 20 set genes.

Network Coverage: number of networks containing with at least 20 set genes. AUPRC, Performance, Performance Gain metrics: median metric of a gene set across all networks containing at least 20 set genes.

experiment.perturbation: observational; network propagation-based gene set recovery
experiment.measurement: gene set size, network coverage, AUPRC, Performance, Performance Gain

text: Controlling for gene set coverage in a subset of 16 interactomes by comparing the 'original' gene set present in each interactome to a 'reduced' maximal subset present in all 16, the authors relate gene set recovery performance to interactome interaction count with log-linear fits and report distributions of regression slopes for Literature and Genetic gene sets.

quotes.quote: (B, C) Gene set recovery performance for a subset of 16 interactomes, controlling for gene set coverage. Given a set of disease-associated genes, the “original” set represents the genes present in each interactome independently, while the “reduced” set represents the maximal subset of genes present in all 16 interactomes.
(C) Distribution of regression slopes between interactome size and gene set recovery performance for Literature and Genetic gene sets, as calculated for size-adjusted performance.

experiment.perturbation: gene set coverage controlled by restricting to genes present in all 16 interactomes
experiment.measurement: mean gene set recovery performance versus interaction count; log-linear regression slopes with 95% confidence intervals

text: Interaction-type-specific interactomes were defined from HumanNet and GeneMANIA, some of which could not be defined from available data, and their interaction similarities were measured by the Jaccard Index of network interactions and clustered with the Ward variance minimization algorithm.

quotes.quote: (D) Sizes of interaction-type-speciﬁc interactomes deﬁned from HumanNet and GeneMANIA. Crosses indicate that a network could not be deﬁned from available data.
(E) Interaction similarities of interaction-type-speciﬁc networks. Similarities measured by the Jaccard Index of network interactions, and clustered using the Ward variance minimization algorithm.

experiment.measurement: network sizes and pairwise Jaccard Index of interactions with Ward clustering

quotes.quote: (A, B) Distribution of the fraction of CORUM (A) and PANTHER (B) interactions present in each interactome. Interactomes with the highest overlap are labeled. (C, D) Interaction prediction performance (mean of P@k using the MPS algorithm) as a function of interaction overlap with CORUM (C) and PANTHER (D), with associated Pearson’s correlation value.

experiment.perturbation: observational
experiment.measurement: fraction of external interactions covered; mean P@k from MPS link prediction; Pearson correlation between overlap and performance

text: Protein assemblies predicted by hierarchical community detection in each interactome were evaluated by the number of CORUM complexes recovered, defined as CORUM complexes with a Jaccard similarity of ≥0.5 with any predicted assembly, and by functional coherency and clustering coefficients of assemblies with fewer than 200 proteins, with the 15 top-performing networks shown per metric.

(F) Number of CORUM complexes recovered, deﬁned as the number of CORUM complexes with a Jaccard similarity of ≥0.5 with any predicted assembly. (G) Functional coherency of predicted assemblies with fewer than 200 proteins based on the mean semantic similarity of GO annotations between assembly proteins (Methods). (H) Distribution of clustering coefﬁcients of predicted assemblies with fewer than 200 proteins.

assembly size cutoff for coherency/clustering analysis

text: Previously unreported predicted interactions classified as AF-supported form a subnetwork in which node color indicates broad protein function and edge color indicates the predicting interactome, with some protein pairs linked by multiple edges because they were predicted in the top 50 previously unreported interactions by multiple networks.

quotes.quote:
Subnetwork of all previously unreported interactions classiﬁed as AF-supported.
Node color indicates broad protein function and edge color indicates the predicting interactome. Protein pairs linked by multiple edges were predicted in the top 50 previously unreported interactions by multiple networks.

experiment.perturbation: AlphaFold-based structural assessment of predicted pairs

text: Mitochondrially-targeted OGG1 transgenic mice were resistant to LPS-induced ARDS, with reduced lung damage and less IL-1β in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid but no change in TNF secretion.

quotes.quote:
mt-Ogg1Tg mice were resistant to LPS-induced ARDS, displaying reduced pulmonary 
vascular endothelium damage, interstitial edema, macrophage and neutrophil infiltration 
alveolar wall thickening and collagen deposition (Figures 1A and 1B). Fittingly, mt-Ogg1Tg 
mice had less IL-1β in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) but no change in TNF secretion

experiment.system: mt-Ogg1Tg and WT mice
experiment.perturbation: LPS-induced ARDS (5 mg/kg LPS i.p., 24 h)
experiment.measurement: lung histology/immunohistochemistry and BALF IL-1β and TNF ELISA

text: mt-Ogg1Tg mice were resistant to alum-induced peritonitis, with reduced IL-1β and neutrophil and monocyte infiltration and little change in TNF.

quotes.quote:
Alum-challenged mt-Ogg1Tg mice exhibited reduced IL-1β and neutrophil 
and monocyte infiltration relative to wildtype (WT) counterparts, with little change in tumor 
necrosis factor (TNF).

experiment.system: mt-Ogg1Tg and WT mice
experiment.perturbation: i.p. alum challenge
experiment.measurement: peritoneal cytokine ELISA and flow cytometry of neutrophils/monocytes

text: ATP-challenged mt-Ogg1Tg BMDM had less 8-oxoG-containing Ox-mtDNA in cytoplasm and mitochondria and lower cytosolic mtDNA, while Ogg1−/− macrophages had more of both.

quotes.quote:
ATP-challenged mt-Ogg1Tg BMDM had less 
8-oxoG-containing Ox-mtDNA in cytoplasm and mitochondria than WT counterparts 
(Figure 1D), whereas ATP-challenged Ogg1−/−-macrophages had more Ox-mtDNA in 
both compartments

Cytosolic mtDNA was also lower 
in mt-Ogg1Tg (Figure 1G), and higher in Ogg1−/− (Figures 1H and S1E) macrophages 
that were ATP challenged.

experiment.system: LPS-primed WT, mt-Ogg1Tg and Ogg1−/− BMDM
experiment.perturbation: ATP (4 mM, 1 h) challenge
experiment.measurement: 8-OH-dG ELISA of mtDNA and qPCR of cytosolic mtDNA

text: mtOGG1 overexpression or loss had no effect on the LPS-stimulated mtDNA increase, implying mtOGG1 interferes with mtDNA oxidation but not synthesis.

quotes.quote:
mtOGG1 overexpression or lack thereof had no effect on the 
LPS-stimulated mtDNA increase (Figures S1F–S1H), implying that mtOGG1 interferes with 
mtDNA oxidation, but not synthesis.

experiment.system: mt-Ogg1Tg and Ogg1−/− BMDM
experiment.perturbation: LPS priming
experiment.measurement: qPCR of total mtDNA

text: mtOGG1 inhibited Casp1 activation, pro-IL-1β processing and ASC speck formation in LPS-primed BMDM stimulated with ATP, nigericin, MSU or alum, whereas Ogg1 ablation had the opposite effect, with no effect on TNF secretion or inflammasome component expression.

quotes.quote:
mtOGG1 inhibited Casp1 activation and 
pro-IL-1β processing in LPS-primed BMDM stimulated with ATP, nigericin, monosodium 
urate (MSU), or alum (Figures 1I, 1J and S1I), whereas Ogg1 ablation had the opposite 
effect (Figures 1K, S1J and S1K). OGG1 had no effect on TNF secretion or pro-IL-1β 
and NLRP3 inflammasome component expression

ASC speck 
formation, reflecting inflammasome assembly (Dick et al., 2016), was also inhibited in 
mt-Ogg1Tg BMDM

experiment.system: LPS-primed WT, mt-Ogg1Tg, Ogg1−/− BMDM
experiment.perturbation: NLRP3 activators ATP, nigericin, MSU, alum
experiment.measurement: immunoblot of Casp1 p20/mature IL-1β, ELISA, ASC speck immunofluorescence

text: ATP challenge induced VDAC oligomerization in LPS-primed BMDM, which was blocked by the VDAC1 oligomerization inhibitor VBIT-4.

quotes.quote:
In LPS-primed BMDM, 
VDAC oligomerization was induced by ATP challenge, indicating channel opening, and 
blocked by VBIT-4, a VDAC1 oligomerization inhibitor (Figure 2A).

experiment.system: LPS-primed BMDM
experiment.perturbation: ATP challenge ± VBIT-4
experiment.measurement: EGS cross-linking and anti-VDAC immunoblot

text: ATP challenge induced mPTP opening (decreased calcein fluorescence), which was blocked by cyclosporine A; VBIT-4 had little effect on calcein fluorescence.

quotes.quote:
ATP challenge induced mPTP opening, suggested by markedly 
decreased calcein fluorescence (Figure 2B). The mPTP inhibitor cyclosporine A (CsA)

blocked the decrease in calcein fluorescence and increased it above baseline 
(Figure 2B), suggesting low basal mPTP opening. However, the VDAC oligomerization 
inhibitor VBIT-4 had little effect on calcein fluorescence.

experiment.system: BMDM
experiment.perturbation: ATP challenge ± CsA or VBIT-4
experiment.measurement: calcein-quenching assay of mPTP opening

text: mtOGG1 overexpression or ablation had no effect on VDAC oligomerization or mPTP opening.

quotes.quote:
mtOGG1 overexpression or ablation had no effect on VDAC 
oligomerization (Figure S2A) or mPTP opening (Figures S2B and S2C)

experiment.system: mt-Ogg1Tg and Ogg1-deficient BMDM
experiment.perturbation: NLRP3 activator challenge
experiment.measurement: VDAC cross-linking immunoblot and calcein assay

text: CsA reduced cytosolic Ox-mtDNA by 60± 6% and mtDNA by 30–40%, and VBIT-4 reduced cytosolic Ox-mtDNA by 81± 4% and mtDNA by 50–60%, even in Ogg1-silenced BMDM.

quotes.quote:
inhibition of mPTP opening with CsA reduced the cytosolic pools of Ox-mtDNA by 60± 
6% and mtDNA by 30–40%, and VDAC oligomerization inhibition with VBIT-4 reduced 
cytosolic Ox-mtDNA by 81± 4% and mtDNA by 50–60%, even in Ogg1-silenced BMDM

experiment.system: LPS-primed shCtrl/shOgg1 BMDM
experiment.perturbation: ATP challenge with CsA or VBIT-4 pretreatment
experiment.measurement: cytosolic Ox-mtDNA (8-OH-dG ELISA) and mtDNA qPCR

text: mtDNA depletion with ethidium bromide did not block VDAC oligomerization, indicating VDAC oligomerization does not require mtDNA.

quotes.quote:
mtDNA depletion with ethidium bromide (EtBr) did not block VDAC oligomerization 
(Figures 2E, S2D and S2E). Thus, VDAC oligomerization and opening do not require 
mtDNA.

experiment.system: BMDM treated with EtBr (450 ng/mL, 4 days)
experiment.perturbation: ATP incubation for 1, 2 or 3 h
experiment.measurement: VDAC cross-linking immunoblot

text: In proteinase K-treated mitochondria, intermembrane space Ox-mtDNA and mtDNA were greatly reduced by CsA but elevated by VBIT-4, and the CsA effect was dominant, indicating Ox-mtDNA exits the IMM via an mPTP-dependent pore before reaching the cytoplasm through VDAC.

quotes.quote:
The amounts of Ox-mtDNA (Figure 2G) 
and different regions of the mtDNA genome (Figure 2H) within the IMS were greatly 
reduced after blocking mPTP opening with CsA but were elevated after inhibition of 
VDAC oligomerization with VBIT-4. Importantly, the CsA effect was dominant to that 
of VBIT-4, indicating that Ox-mtDNA first exited the IMM via an mPTP-dependent pore 
and then reached the cytoplasm through VDAC channels.

experiment.system: purified mitochondria from BMDM
experiment.perturbation: CsA and/or VBIT-4 treatment; proteinase K (20 μg/mL, 30 min) OMM rupture
experiment.measurement: Ox-mtDNA and mtDNA quantification in IMS fraction

text: CsA and VBIT-4 inhibited NLRP3 inflammasome activation in WT and Ogg1−/− BMDM without affecting NLRP3, pro-IL-1β, pro-casp1 and ASC expression or TNF secretion; Vdac1 or Vdac3 silencing also prevented Casp1 activation and mature IL-1β secretion, and VBIT-4 inhibited ASC speck formation.

quotes.quote:
Both CsA and VBIT-4 inhibited 
NLRP3 inflammasome activation in WT and Ogg1−/−- BMDM, without affecting NLRP3, 
pro-IL-1β, pro-casp1 and ASC expression or TNF secretion (Figures 2I–2K, S2G and S2H). 
Vdac1 or Vdac3 silencing also prevented Casp1 activation and mature IL-1β secretion 
(Figure S2I), and ASC speck formation was inhibited by VBIT-4

experiment.system: LPS-primed WT and Ogg1−/− BMDM; shVdac1/shVdac3-transduced BMDM
experiment.perturbation: CsA, VBIT-4 or Vdac silencing with NLRP3 activator challenge
experiment.measurement: immunoblot of Casp1 p20/IL-1β, ELISA, ASC speck imaging

text: CsA and VBIT-4 reduced mtDNA oxidation by 33 ± 7.5% and 45 ± 5.0%, respectively, presumably due to a modest decline in mtROS production.

quotes.quote:
CsA and VBIT-4 reduced mtDNA oxidation by 33 ± 7.5% and 45 ± 5.0%, respectively 
(Figure S2J), presumably due to a modest decline in mtROS production (Figure S2K).

experiment.system: BMDM
experiment.perturbation: CsA or VBIT-4 pretreatment with NLRP3 activator challenge
experiment.measurement: mtDNA oxidation (8-OH-dG) and MitoSOX mtROS

text: CsA or VBIT-4 abrogated mitochondrial depolarization upon NLRP3 activator challenge.

quotes.quote:
BMDM 
incubated with CsA, or VBIT-4 abrogated mitochondrial depolarization upon NLRP3 
activator challenge (Figure S2L)

experiment.system: BMDM
experiment.perturbation: CsA or VBIT-4 with NLRP3 activator challenge
experiment.measurement: TMRM mitochondrial membrane potential

text: Nigericin, MSU and alum, even without LPS priming, triggered VDAC oligomerization and mPTP opening.

quotes.quote:
BMDM exposure to nigericin, MSU and alum, even without LPS priming, also triggered 
VDAC oligomerization (Figures 3A and 3B) and mPTP opening (Figure 3C)

experiment.system: BMDM ± LPS priming
experiment.perturbation: nigericin, MSU, alum challenge
experiment.measurement: VDAC cross-linking immunoblot and calcein-quenching assay

text: NLRP3 activators strongly elevated mitochondrial Ca2+ (Rhod-2) with a rapid [Ca2+]m spike within 30–50 sec of agonist challenge, unaffected by mtOGG1 overexpression or deficiency.

quotes.quote:
Rhod-2 (a 
dye that fluoresces in response to mitochondrial Ca2+ binding) fluorescence in BMDM 
stimulated with different NLRP3 activators, with or without LPS priming, was strongly 
elevated (Figures 3D and S3A). A rapid [Ca2+]m spike was detected within 30–50 sec of 
NLRP3 agonist challenge (Figure 3E)

mtOGG1 overexpression or deficiency had no impact 
on [Ca2+]m uptake amplitude

experiment.system: BMDM (WT, mt-Ogg1Tg, Ogg1-deficient)
experiment.perturbation: ATP, nigericin, MSU or alum challenge
experiment.measurement: Rhod-2 fluorescence live imaging/plate reader

text: CsA inhibition of mPTP opening suppressed VDAC oligomerization, indicating mPTP opening triggers VDAC oligomerization.

quotes.quote:
inhibition of mPTP opening 
with CsA suppressed VDAC oligomerization (Figure 3F), indicating that mPTP opening 
triggerred VDAC oligomerization.

experiment.system: BMDM
experiment.perturbation: CsA pretreatment, LPS priming, ATP stimulation
experiment.measurement: VDAC cross-linking immunoblot

text: No cytochrome C release was observed during NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and etoposide, which induced cytochrome C release, did not trigger ASC speck formation.

quotes.quote:
No cytochrome C release was observed during NLRP3 
inflammasome activation and etoposide, which induced cytochrome C release, did not 
trigger ASC speck formation (Figure S3D)

experiment.system: BMDM
experiment.perturbation: NLRP3 activators vs etoposide (10 μg/mL, 16 h)

text: The mtROS generators DMNQ and mitoParaquat produced as much mtROS as ATP and augmented mtDNA oxidation but induced neither mPTP opening, VDAC oligomerization, cytosolic Ox-mtDNA/mtDNA release, nor NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

quotes.quote:
Although producing as much mtROS as ATP (Figure S3E), 
neither compound induced mPTP opening (Figure S3F), VDAC oligomerization (Figure 
S3G) and consequent Ox-mtDNA (Figure S3H) and mtDNA (Figure S3I) cytosolic release. 
While mtDNA oxidation was augmented (Figure S3H), neither mtROS generator activated 
NLRP3 inflammasome (Figure S3J).

experiment.system: BMDM
experiment.perturbation: DMNQ (20 μM) or MitoParaquat (5 μM) treatment
experiment.measurement: MitoSOX mtROS, calcein mPTP assay, VDAC cross-linking, cytosolic mtDNA qPCR, inflammasome immunoblot

text: The MCU inhibitor ruthenium red disrupted the ATP- or nigericin-induced mitochondrial Ca2+ pulse whereas the IP3R antagonist xestospongin C had no effect on it, though XeC decreased cytosolic Ca2+.

quotes.quote:
Whereas RuR disrupted the ATP- or nigericin-induced [Ca2+]m pulse (Figure 4A), 
XeC had no effect, although it decreased cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure S4A).

experiment.perturbation: XeC (5 μM) or RuR (10 μM) pretreatment, ATP or nigericin challenge
experiment.measurement: Rhod-2 and Fluo-4 fluorescence

text: RuR blocked mPTP opening and VDAC oligomerization, reduced cytosolic Ox-mtDNA and mtDNA release, and suppressed Casp1 activation and mature IL-1β secretion without affecting LPS-stimulated mtDNA synthesis, inflammasome component expression or TNF secretion.

quotes.quote:
RuR 
blocked mPTP opening (Figure 4B) and VDAC oligomerization (Figures 4C and S4B), 
reducing cytosolic Ox-mtDNA (Figure 4D) and cytoplasmic mtDNA release (Figure 4E). 
RuR did not inhibit LPS-stimulated mtDNA synthesis (Figure S4C), but it suppressed Casp1 
activation and mature IL-1β secretion (Figures 4F, 4G and S4D), with no effect on NLRP3 
inflammasome component expression (Figure 4H) or TNF secretion (Figure 4G).

experiment.system: LPS-primed BMDM
experiment.perturbation: RuR (10 μM, 16 h) pretreatment with NLRP3 activator challenge
experiment.measurement: calcein assay, VDAC cross-linking, cytosolic mtDNA/Ox-mtDNA, immunoblot and ELISA

text: Nigericin or ATP treatment of LPS-primed BMDM produced cytoplasmic DNA at 500–650 bp while most mitochondrial mtDNA remained >5 kb; this cytoplasmic DNA was absent in EtBr-treated cells and no nuclear DNA degradation was seen.

quotes.quote:
Although the majority of mtDNA remaining within mitochondria was >5 kb, nigericin 
and ATP treatments led to appearance of cytoplasmic DNA at 500–650 bp in length (Figure 
5A). This DNA was mitochondrially derived because it was absent in EtBr-treated BMDM 
(Figures S5A and S5B). Nuclear DNA degradation was not observed
